# Wisdom of Solomon Chapter 13 — The PNEUMA Bible (Dynamic)
**Translator:** PNEUMA | **Source:** Codex Vaticanus, Wisdom 13 | **Source Image:** source-texts/greek-DC/WIS_013_page_001.jpg

---

**13:1** All people who remain ignorant of God are simply foolish — because from the visible, beautiful things around them they should have been able to know the One Who Truly Is, and by studying his works they should have recognized the maker. But they failed.

**13:2** Instead, they decided that gods were running the universe — fire, or wind, or swirling air, or the wheeling stars, or the surge of water, or the bright lights of the sky.

**13:3** If the beauty of these things was what captivated them — fine; but let them understand that their Master is far more wonderful than any of it, because the one who made them is the very Author of beauty itself.

**13:4** And if they were overwhelmed by the power and energy of these things, let them work out the logic: how much more powerful must the one be who brought them into existence?

**13:5** Because from the greatness and beauty of created things, you can catch a proportional glimpse of their Creator.

**13:6** Still, these people deserve only a moderate blame; maybe they went astray while genuinely looking for God, genuinely wanting to find him.

**13:7** They live surrounded by his handiwork, they study it, they look at it — and the visible world is undeniably beautiful, so they stop there, convinced by what they see.

**13:8** But they still have no excuse.

**13:9** If they were intelligent enough to speculate about the whole cosmos, how could they have failed to find its Master sooner?

**13:10** But the truly wretched ones — the ones whose hope is deposited in dead things — are those who call human handiwork their gods: gold, silver, clever craft-work, likenesses of animals, or some useless stone chiseled out by some craftsman long ago.

**13:11** Imagine a woodcutter who fells a good tree, strips its bark carefully, trims all the awkward, twisted branches, and works the timber into something practical — a useful vessel for everyday needs.

**13:12** The wood chips and scraps go on the fire; he cooks his dinner over them.

**13:13** But there's a piece left over — warped, knotted, completely useless. He picks it up in his spare time, and with careful, practiced skill he carves it into the shape of a person,

**13:14** or makes it look like some insignificant animal, then slathers it with red paint, covers the whole surface in crimson, hides every crack and flaw under a coat of color —

**13:15** and then builds a little shrine for it, mounts it on the wall, nails it in place.

**13:16** He makes sure to nail it in carefully, because he knows it cannot hold itself up. It is just a carving — it needs help.

**13:17** And then — he is not embarrassed in the least — he prays to this dead thing about his property, his marriage, his children. He appeals to something without any strength at all to help him get healthy.

**13:18** He begs a corpse to give him life. He asks for help from something that has never had a moment of experience. He requests travel assistance from something that has never taken a step.

**13:19** For profit, for business success, for skillful hands — he asks for capability from something whose own hands are utterly incapable of anything.
